## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Within days of the M7.5 earthquake that struck coastal Venezuela on 24 June 2026, at least
eight satellite-derived building-damage products were released by government, academic,
UN, and private-sector providers, differing in sensor, method, coverage, and format. We
evaluate six of them against a three-way reference framework with deliberately disjoint
failure modes: expert-interpreted damage points from Copernicus EMS (both false alarms and
misses, within its mapped extents), a crowdsourced MapSwipe validation campaign (false
alarms only), and ground-reported ChatMap field points (misses only). Three results
organise the evaluation. First, although every product is a poor per-building classifier
(precision floors 0.03–0.12 against a heavily over-detecting background), all rank *areas*
by damage burden well, and their residual error is spatially aligned with shaking severity
rather than with confounders such as building density — the benign error structure that
preserves ranking. Second, per-building performance cannot be tuned into existence within
a single product — a threshold sweep of a purpose-built SAR change product, Microsoft's own
confidence axis, and same-sensor consensus all plateau at a common "modality floor" — but
combining products across sensor modalities steps over it: agreement count behaves as a
calibrated confidence dial, trading field-verified coverage (97%→18%) against
visits-per-verified-find (26.5→0.8), and a simple learned weighting of the six products
improves on flat voting by a further 40% under spatially blocked cross-validation. The
sobering baseline: a model given only geography (coastline distance, building density,
shaking intensity) predicts damaged buildings as well as the best individual satellite
product. Third, all products, and the expert reference itself, detect *destruction* far
better than lighter damage: Copernicus EMS matched 94% of field-reported "complete"
destruction but only 49% of "significant" damage, implying that published precision figures
for such products are systematically understated. We close with an operational tiering and
its costs, presented as a responder's decision rather than a recommendation.

## Introduction

In the first hours to days after a major earthquake, responders need to know *where the
damage is and how bad*, before ground access is possible. Satellite-derived damage products
fill this window, and their supply has grown dramatically: the 2026 Venezuela earthquake
drew products from a government rapid-mapping service (Copernicus EMS), academic SAR groups
(Oregon State University; IMPACT Initiatives' Sentinel-1 analysis), optical AI pipelines
(Microsoft AI for Good; University of Houston; a WFP/LIST/CERN collaboration), debris-mass
modelling (UNEP/OCHA Joint Environment Unit), and volunteer AI platforms (HOT fAIr, DISHA).
These products disagree — sometimes spectacularly — and a coordinator receiving them in the
same week has no established way to know which to trust, for what, and at what spatial
scale.

The evaluation literature typically scores such products against expert-interpreted
reference data as if the reference were complete truth and as if per-building accuracy were
the only question. Both assumptions fail operationally. A product with abundant false
positives may still direct response correctly if its errors are spatially benign; and the
expert reference itself, produced under the same time pressure, has measurable gaps. We
therefore ask three questions, each mapped to a decision a responder actually faces:

1. **Where?** Do products rank areas (neighbourhoods, districts) by damage burden
   correctly, even when their per-building labels are noisy?
2. **Which buildings?** Can any product, or combination, produce a per-building list
   accurate enough to act on — and at what verification cost?
3. **What does everything miss?** Where do all products, and the reference itself, fail —
   and how would a responder know?

Our contribution is threefold: a **multi-reference evaluation framework** in which three
independent reference datasets with disjoint failure modes cross-check one another; the
empirical demonstration of a **modality floor** — the limit that single-sensor tuning
cannot cross but cross-modal consensus can; and a quantified **operational tiering** that
prices the trade between coverage and wasted verification effort instead of declaring a
single winner.

## The event and the products

An M7.5 earthquake (preceded ~40 s by an M7.2) struck near Yumare, coastal Venezuela, at
22:05 UTC on 24 June 2026, with severe damage concentrated along the La Guaira coastal
strip, in western Caracas, and in several inland towns. Copernicus EMS rapid mapping was
activated (EMSR884) the same night.

We evaluate the six products with a defined or defensible *analysed extent* — the area the
product actually examined, without which neither misses nor false-alarm rates can be fairly
counted (@tbl-products). Two further AI products (HOT fAIr, DISHA) lacked any analysed
extent and are included in the availability inventory only. All products were harmonised
onto a common base of Overture building footprints for combination analyses (each footprint
"flagged" by a product if that product's damage evidence intersects it), while all
*scoring* against references uses each product's native geometry — a separation we return
to in Methods.

| Product | Provider | Sensing basis | Analysed buildings | Damage flags* |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft AI4G | Microsoft | very-high-res optical + AI classifier | 72,162 (own footprints) | 8,410 |
| IMPACT v2 | IMPACT Initiatives | Sentinel-1 radar coherence change | swath (~372 km²) | 22,954 |
| OSU | Oregon State Univ. / NASA | Sentinel-1 radar coherence change | swath (~471 km²) | 31,259 |
| UH QuakeDamage | Univ. of Houston | optical imagery + vision model, graded footprints | 447,263 incl. intact | ~91k dmg/destroyed |
| LIST | WFP / LIST / CERN | ResNet pre/post model | 163,225 | 15,904 in core region |
| UNEP debris | UNEP/OCHA JEU | SAR-derived debris mass per footprint | no extent (assumption, see Methods) | 96,046 |

: Products evaluated. *Flag counts as harmonised to the common footprint base within each
product's own region; totals differ from providers' native counts due to footprint-base
differences. {#tbl-products}

**A note on radar vs optical sensing**, since it matters later. Optical products (Microsoft,
UH, LIST) classify what damage *looks like* from above. Radar (SAR) products exploit a
different physical quantity: *coherence*, the stability of the microscopic arrangement of
radar scatterers within each pixel between satellite passes. Intact buildings are rigid
reflector arrangements (high coherence); collapse rearranges them (coherence drops).
Vegetation, by contrast, never holds coherence — so radar coherence methods are largely
blind to farmland and forest change that fools amplitude- or optical-based methods, a
property we verify empirically below.

## Reference data: three datasets, three failure modes

No single reference dataset can score both the false alarms and the misses of these
products everywhere. We therefore triangulate three:

**Copernicus EMS (CEMS) building-damage points** — trained analysts visually interpreting
very-high-resolution imagery, marking each damaged building as a graded point. Within its
mapped extents this is reference-grade for both error types, under one explicit assumption:
that a building *without* a CEMS point, inside an area CEMS analysed, is genuinely
undamaged. We use the latest monitoring product per area (3,119 points; 1,467 damaged or
destroyed within the core comparison region) and treat its two known bounds — coverage
(truth only inside its extents) and grade (see Results C) — explicitly.

**MapSwipe crowd validation** — a Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team campaign in which 400+
volunteers were shown ~8,000 locations *where an AI product had flagged damage* and voted
"damaged / no damage / not sure" on each (~50 m hexagonal cells; median 6–13 votes per
cell). Because volunteers only ever saw AI-flagged places, this dataset can adjudicate
**false alarms but never misses**.

**ChatMap field reports** — 415 ground-reported damage points collected by field teams,
graded minimal/significant/complete. Ground observation makes each point strong evidence of
damage, but the collection is opportunistic (no defined survey area), so absence of a point
means nothing: this dataset measures **misses but never false alarms**. Notably, its points
extend inland beyond every CEMS extent.

The three failure modes interlock: CEMS is two-sided but bounded; MapSwipe covers the
false-alarm side of AI flags; ChatMap covers the miss side anywhere. Each is used only for
the question it can answer.

## Methods

### Matching products to references: dual-anchored, native-geometry scoring

Products and references use different geometries (points, polygons, rasters) on different
footprint bases, so any comparison needs a matching rule. We use **dual-anchored matching**:
recall and precision are computed from *opposite anchors*, so no count of true negatives —
the vast, uninformative stock of undamaged buildings — is ever needed.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Dual-anchored matching. Left: a product is scored only where it AND the reference both looked. Middle: recall anchors on the reference — each CEMS damage point asks whether a product flag lies within radius r. Right: precision anchors on the product — each flagged building asks whether a CEMS point lies within r. Each metric brings its own denominator."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mp
import numpy as np
from shapely.geometry import Point

R = 0.16
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 5.1))
a0 = ax[0]
c1, c2 = Point(-0.28, 0).buffer(0.75), Point(0.28, 0).buffer(0.75)
inter = c1.intersection(c2)
a0.add_patch(mp.Polygon(np.asarray(inter.exterior.coords), closed=True, fc="#c8e6c9", ec="none"))
for c, col, lab, xy in ((c1, "tab:blue", "CEMS analysed extent", (-0.75, 0.62)),
                        (c2, "tab:orange", "product AOI", (0.42, 0.62))):
    a0.add_patch(mp.Polygon(np.asarray(c.exterior.coords), closed=True, fc="none", ec=col, lw=2))
    a0.annotate(lab, xy, fontsize=9, color=col)
a0.annotate("scored HERE only", (0, -0.05), fontsize=10, ha="center", weight="bold", color="#2e7d32")
a0.set_title("1 · where scoring happens", fontsize=10)
a1 = ax[1]
for x, y in [(-0.38, 0.22), (0.05, -0.32), (-0.6, -0.5), (0.62, -0.15)]:
    a1.scatter(x, y, marker="s", s=70, c="tab:orange", zorder=3)
for x, y, hit in [(-0.45, 0.3, True), (0.15, -0.25, True), (0.45, 0.42, False)]:
    a1.add_patch(mp.Circle((x, y), R, fc="none", ec="grey", ls="--"))
    a1.scatter(x, y, marker="*", s=180, c="k", zorder=4)
    a1.annotate("TP" if hit else "FN (missed)", (x + 0.05, y + 0.13), fontsize=9,
                color="#2e7d32" if hit else "#c62828", weight="bold")
a1.set_title("2 · RECALL — anchor on each CEMS point", fontsize=10)
a2 = ax[2]
for x, y in [(-0.36, 0.25), (0.2, -0.14)]:
    a2.scatter(x, y, marker="*", s=180, c="k", zorder=4)
for x, y, hit in [(-0.45, 0.32, True), (0.1, -0.2, True), (0.5, 0.45, False), (-0.15, -0.6, False)]:
    a2.add_patch(mp.Circle((x, y), R, fc="none", ec="grey", ls="--"))
    a2.scatter(x, y, marker="s", s=70, c="tab:orange", zorder=3)
    a2.annotate("TP" if hit else "FP (false alarm)", (x + 0.05, y + 0.13), fontsize=9,
                color="#2e7d32" if hit else "#c62828", weight="bold")
a2.set_title("3 · PRECISION — anchor on each product flag", fontsize=10)
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlim(-1.05, 1.05); a.set_ylim(-1.0, 0.9)
    a.set_aspect("equal"); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
h = [plt.Line2D([], [], marker="*", ls="", ms=13, c="k", label="CEMS damage point"),
     plt.Line2D([], [], marker="s", ls="", ms=8, c="tab:orange", label="product-flagged building"),
     plt.Line2D([], [], ls="--", c="grey", label="match radius r")]
fig.legend(handles=h, loc="lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 0.97))
plt.show()
```

A product is only accountable where it *and* the reference both looked, so all scoring is
restricted to the intersection of analysed extents. UNEP debris publishes no extent; per an
explicit, stated assumption (supported by its density in the study region) we treat it as
fully covering the ~61 km² core comparison region — the same "enclosure" logic used for its
stand-alone evaluation in fully enclosed administrative units.

Analysed extents bound *where* a product looked, not whether it could *see*: cloud can
obscure individual buildings inside a declared extent. Only one product (Microsoft)
publishes a per-building visibility field, and a robustness check against it shows the
effect is negligible in this event — 3.6% of buildings are majority-obscured, precision is
unchanged under any visibility filter, and exactly one missed reference point falls on an
obscured building (the model abstains under cloud rather than flagging into it). We
therefore score all products without visibility corrections, noting that the check itself
is impossible for the five products that publish no such field.

**The matching radius is derived from the urban fabric, not chosen for leniency.** The
median distance between neighbouring building centroids in the core region is **9.7 m**
(93% of buildings have a neighbour within 20 m). We therefore use r = 10 m as the largest
radius at which "did the product flag *this* building" remains answerable, and treat larger
radii as answers to a *different*, equally legitimate question — did the flag put a
responder where damage is visible or findable — with named scales: 30 m (line of sight),
60 m (same block), 100 m (right area).

### Area ranking and error structure

For the "where" question we aggregate per-building flags to hexagonal grid cells (Uber's H3
indexing system) at two sizes — ≈0.74 km² and ≈5.2 km², the latter approximating a triage
sector — and compare each product's cell ranking against CEMS's using rank correlation and
top-k concordance (the overlap between the product's and the reference's k worst-hit cells).

Whether ranking *survives* noise depends on the noise's spatial structure, so we test it
directly. A Poisson regression predicts each cell's product-flag count from its CEMS damage
count, with the cell's total building stock as an *exposure offset* — meaning the model
scores each cell's per-building flagging **rate**, so that "more flags because more
buildings" cannot masquerade as bias. The regression's residuals — over- or under-flagging
unexplained by true damage — are then tested two ways: for spatial clumping with **Moran's
I** (a statistic near 0 when values are arranged randomly across cells and positive when
similar values cluster; significance from 999 random re-shufflings of the values over the
*same* cell lattice, which conditions out the shape of the built area itself), and for
association with non-damage covariates (building density, distance to coast, modelled
shaking intensity) that would indicate rank-corrupting bias.

### Consensus voting and its adjudication

For the "which buildings" question, each product's flags are projected onto the shared
Overture footprint base and combined by **k-of-6 voting**: a building is flagged by the
rule when at least k of the six products flag it. Throughout, "k-of-6" names a *rule*,
never a score. Voting rules are then scored exactly as single products are — construction
happens on the shared base; scoring remains native-geometry dual-anchor.

Because CEMS itself has gaps, precision measured against CEMS is a **floor**. We quantify
how far below truth that floor sits by *adjudicating* each rule's CEMS-unmatched flags
against the MapSwipe crowd: for every flagged building with no CEMS point within 10 m, we
look up the crowd's majority verdict for its ~50 m cell (requiring ≥4 votes) and count the
share judged damaged.

## Results A — one product tells you *where*

Scored per building at identity scale (r = 10 m), every product is weak: recall against
CEMS damage ranges 0.31–0.69 across the six members, while precision floors sit at
0.03–0.12, reflecting over-detection of roughly 6–26 flags per CEMS damage point. Read
naively, these numbers say the products are unusable. Read operationally, they say
per-building labels are the wrong unit for single products — because the *area* signal is
strong:

- At triage-sector scale, Microsoft and OSU place **80–85% of the 20 worst-hit cells**
  correctly (rank correlation ρ ≈ 0.57), despite their over-detection. Skill improves as
  cells coarsen: the noise averages out.
- The error-structure test explains why. Residual over-flagging is spatially clumped
  (Moran's I 0.45–0.60, p = 0.001 throughout — the errors are *not* random noise), but once
  building stock is controlled, the clumping follows **the earthquake itself**: it rises
  toward the coast and with modelled shaking intensity, and shows no association with
  building density. Products over-call most *where the damage really is worst* — an error
  structure that preserves, arguably sharpens, area rankings; the dangerous alternative
  (errors tracking urban form) is what the test rules out.

![Exposure-adjusted residual maps (red = over-flagging beyond what CEMS damage explains).
IMPACT and OSU's residuals follow the coastal severity gradient; Microsoft's error is one
hard localized cluster at the west end of its
region.](artefacts/RQ3-prioritization-error-structure/figs/rq3_residual_maps_res8.png)

The exception proves the method. Microsoft's residual error is not a gradient but one hard
cluster in the western coastal strip, unexplained by any covariate. Two rival explanations
— genuine false positives vs CEMS under-recording there — are separable with the crowd
data: in that strip, volunteers judged **71% of Microsoft-flagged locations "no damage"**
(versus a 49/48 split in the damage-dense east). Independent humans looking at post-event
imagery mostly saw nothing where the cluster flags damage: the cluster is real
over-detection, not reference failure.

The product's own metadata then completes the diagnosis — and generalizes it. Every
building in the western strip carries `num_observations = 1`: the zone was covered by
exactly one satellite scene, and the platform behind the product (HASTE; Robinson, Ortiz
et al. 2026) trains a *fresh model per scene*, with cross-scene agreement as the only
internal check — a check the west never received. Cloud cover is ruled out as the
alternative mechanism (the west is the *most* cloud-free zone; a per-building visibility
check moved no metric). Splitting the product at the scene boundary shows what one headline
number was hiding: the single-scene west flags 28.7% of its buildings for precision 0.05
(F1 = 0.10), while the multi-scene east flags 7.6% for precision 0.21 (F1 = 0.30) — the
best single-product zone we measured *anywhere*, inside the same product that produced the
worst. Scoring the two overlapping scenes head-to-head on their ~24,700 shared buildings
sharpens the attribution: the "better" scene's advantage is *restraint* (4.9% vs 27.8%
flagged) rather than accuracy (its flags are crowd-confirmed at 7% vs 14%), and buildings
flagged by *both* scenes are still 72% crowd-rejected in that low-damage zone. The failure
unit is the per-scene model calibration, not the satellite, the provider, or the product.
Two consequences recur throughout this paper: per-product metrics average over regimes
they cannot see, so evaluation should stratify by acquisition provenance wherever it is
published; and it was *only* this product's metadata transparency that made its failure
root-causeable at all — for the other five products we can show that they fail, but never
why.

## Results B — six products tell you *which buildings to check first*

### The modality floor

Could a better single product fix per-building precision? Four independent experiments say
no — the limit is the sensing modality, not the tuning:

1. **Same-sensor consensus plateaus.** Requiring both Sentinel-1 coherence products
   (IMPACT *and* OSU) to agree raises precision only to 0.088 — barely above the single
   products — because products sharing sensor physics share false positives, which voting
   then cannot remove.
2. **A tunable rebuild saturates.** We built our own Sentinel-1 amplitude-change product
   (per-pixel z-scores against a 30-scene pre-event baseline, full threshold sweep). Its
   best F1 ties the best shipped single product, yet no point on its curve approaches the
   consensus rules — and its false positives concentrated in farmland (8.0% of buildings
   flagged in an agricultural control area where CEMS found ~nothing), confirming the
   radar-coherence advantage over amplitude for rural false alarms.
3. **A confidence axis is flat.** Sweeping Microsoft's own continuous damage-fraction score
   trades recall 0.66→0.10 for precision 0.10→0.19: the shipped binary flag already sits
   near its curve's best F1. There is no hidden headroom in the confidence dial.
4. **Within-product corroboration plateaus like same-sensor voting.** Microsoft flags
   corroborated by a second satellite scene carry 2.5× the precision of single-scene calls
   (0.245 vs 0.097) — a real gain, worth publishing — yet it stalls below every cross-modal
   pair (Microsoft ∧ UH reaches 0.372), and in the low-damage scene-overlap zone even
   flags confirmed by *both* scenes were 72% crowd-rejected. Agreement inside one model
   shares that model's calibration failures; only agreement across modalities escapes them.

### Cross-modal voting steps over the floor

Voting across modalities behaves differently, and the mechanism is error *decorrelation*:
an optical model and a radar product rarely make the same mistake, so requiring agreement
removes false positives faster than it removes true detections. The starkest demonstration:
the University of Houston product is the *weakest* single member (precision floor 0.009 on
its full region), yet its pairing with Microsoft is among the *strongest* rules — a bad
classifier with independent errors is a valuable voter. Conversely the same-sensor pair is
the weakest of all fifteen pairings. We state this as mechanism, not recipe: which specific
pairing wins is likely event-dependent; that modality diversity is the active ingredient is
the durable claim.

Scored against all three references simultaneously, agreement count behaves as a
**calibrated confidence dial** — every step from 1-of-6 to 6-of-6 raises both CEMS-floor
and crowd-adjusted precision while lowering coverage, monotonically:

| rule | flags | CEMS precision floor | crowd-adjusted precision | field recall (30 m) | visits per verified find (30 m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1-of-6 (union) | 37,644 | 0.03 | 0.21 | 0.97 | 26.5 |
| 3-of-6 | 9,409 | 0.10 | 0.28 | 0.86 | 7.5 |
| 4-of-6 | 3,347 | 0.19 | 0.38 | 0.67 | 3.4 |
| 6-of-6 | 214 | 0.64 | 0.93 | 0.18 | 0.8 |

: The consensus dial, priced. "Crowd-adjusted precision" folds back the CEMS-unmatched
flags that MapSwipe volunteers judged damaged; "visits per verified find" is the number of
flagged locations a responder must walk to reach one CEMS-verified damage point, at
line-of-sight matching. {#tbl-dial}

Two honest readings of @tbl-dial. **The false-positive cost is real and dominates at low
consensus:** every single product wastes 80–86% of visits even at line-of-sight scale, the
union wastes 89%, and no matching generosity changes this — there are simply many times
more flags than damaged buildings. Only consensus pays the cost down. **And the unanimous
end is an anchor, not an operating point:** 6-of-6 reaches near-certainty (93%
crowd-adjusted precision; its "wasted" visits fall to 3% at line-of-sight scale) but covers
only 18% of damage. Its scientific value is what it proves about the dial's top end — and
about the reference: **81% of unanimous flags unmatched by CEMS were judged damaged by the
crowd**, making full consensus the sharpest available detector of the reference's own gaps.

![Voting-rule frontier against CEMS (four-member version shown; the six-member table above
supersedes the numbers but the geometry is identical): single products lie on a low-precision
envelope no tuning escapes; consensus rules climb away from
it.](artefacts/RQ5-ensemble/figs/rq5_pr_frontier_r10.png)

### Learned fusion, and the geography baseline

Flat voting weights every product equally. As a final step we fitted two simple *stacking*
models — a logistic regression and a random forest — that predict per-building CEMS damage
from the six flags, the products' own confidence fields (Microsoft's damage fraction and
scene count, the graded classes of UH, OSU, IMPACT and LIST), and three context variables
(building density, coastline distance, shaking intensity). Validation is **spatially
blocked**: models are trained and tested on disjoint ~5 km² zones, because neighbouring
buildings share both features and labels, and a conventional random split would leak that
structure and overstate skill. Buildings the crowd judged damaged but CEMS did not record
were excluded from the negative class, so the model is not penalised for finding reference
gaps.

Three results (all out-of-sample). First, **learned weighting works**: average precision
0.36, against 0.26 for flat k-of-6 voting and 0.08–0.09 for the best single products — and
the logistic model matches the forest, meaning the useful signal is additive and an
interpretable weighted vote captures essentially all of it. Second, an ablation confirms
**the skill belongs to the products**: with product features removed, the context-only
model collapses to 0.08; with context removed, products alone reach 0.33 of the full 0.36.
Third — the mirror of that ablation, and the finding we would put on a slide —
**geography alone ties the best single product**: a model that has never seen a satellite
detection, knowing only how far each building is from the coast, how dense its
neighbourhood is, and the modelled shaking, identifies damaged buildings as well as any
individual product evaluated here. At the building level, in this event, every single
product carried roughly the information content of a coastline map. Combination — flat or
learned — is what first clears that bar.

![Learned fusion vs the flat dial: spatially-blocked out-of-fold precision–recall (left)
and what the model weighs (right).](artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/figs/rq8_learned_fusion.png)

## Results C — what everything misses

Scoring every product against the 415 ground-reported field points (each product within its
own analysed extent; r = 20 m to absorb phone-GPS error) reveals the evaluation's most
consequential pattern (@tbl-field): a universal **grade gradient**.

| reference | field recall: complete | significant | minimal |
|---|---|---|---|
| CEMS (expert reference) | **0.94** | **0.49** | 0.17 |
| OSU | 0.92 | 0.71 | 0.21 |
| Microsoft | 0.82 | 0.33 | — |
| IMPACT v2 | 0.73 | 0.46 | 0.25 |
| UH | 0.59 | 0.23 | 0.45 |
| union of six | 0.97 | 0.85 | — |

: Recall against field-reported damage, by field-assessed grade. {#tbl-field}

Every satellite product — and the expert reference itself — detects *destruction* well and
lighter damage poorly. **Copernicus EMS, within its own mapped extents, matched only 49% of
field-reported "significant" damage** (94% of "complete"). Two implications follow. First,
satellite damage detection, as of this event, is empirically *destruction* detection; totals
derived from it undercount the damaged-but-standing stock that dominates shelter needs.
Second, every precision figure published against an expert reference — including ours — is
a floor, biased downward exactly where damage is lighter; our crowd adjudication (Results B)
quantifies the gap independently. The gradient also replicates externally: an independent
evaluation of the same platform that produced the Microsoft product, on the 2023 Turkey
earthquakes (Ramachandran et al. 2025), reports 94% specificity against 43% sensitivity —
the same see-destruction-miss-damage asymmetry on a different event, different geography,
and different imagery, indicating a modality-general property rather than a Venezuela
quirk.

Geography compounds the grade effect: ~11% of field-reported damage points, concentrated in
inland hill communities, had **no product flag within 20 m despite lying inside product
analysed extents** — collective misses where response attention was thinnest, invisible to
any evaluation that never leaves the coast.

![Field-reported damage points coloured by how many of four AOI products flagged damage
within 20 m. The coastal strip glows; the inland cluster was missed by
everyone.](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2_chatmap_found_by.png)

Finally, a cautionary tale on AI products evaluated only where damage is dense: the UH
product's flags in the hard-hit coastal strip carry the *best* per-building precision of
any single product there — while in agricultural control areas where CEMS found essentially
no damage, it flagged up to 27.5% of buildings, in spatially clumped patterns indicating
systematic model failure rather than noise. Single-region validation would have missed
this entirely.

## Discussion

**For responders**, the results compress to three sentences. Any major product, used at
sector scale, ranks where to go first — trust the ranking, not the counts. Per-building
lists become actionable only through cross-modal consensus, and @tbl-dial prices the dial:
choose the operating point by the cost of a wasted visit against the cost of a missed
building — at current performance, that choice, not product selection, is the consequential
decision. Nothing in the current product ecosystem sees lighter damage reliably — plan
shelter assessments accordingly.

**For providers**, three specific findings travel: multi-scene corroboration is worth
surfacing (Microsoft's 2+-scene flags are 2.5× more precise — publish that flag);
raster-to-footprint transfer misplaces detections (LIST's found-rate jumps 0.56→0.86 from
identity to line-of-sight scale — its detections are near damage but on the wrong
footprint); and publishing an analysed extent is what separates evaluable products from
unevaluable ones — two otherwise interesting products could not be scored at all for lack
of one.

The one product we could examine from the inside (Results A) turns those findings into
three process lessons. *Validation must cover the deployed extent*: the failing scene was
precisely the one absent from the provider's labeled validation, and the platform's prior
external evaluation showed the opposite bias (conservative under-flagging in Turkey) —
per-event, per-scene behavior is not predictable from a track record, so spot-checking
convenient scenes certifies nothing about the others. *The correction signal already
exists and goes unused*: crowd volunteers rejected 71% of the failing zone's flags within
days of the mapping campaign, but no channel carried that signal to the provider
mid-activation — a feedback loop that costs nothing to close and would have caught this
event's largest single error mass while reprocessing was still useful. And *auditability
is a product property worth rewarding*: the only failure we could root-cause — and
therefore the only one with a concrete fix — belonged to the most transparent product.
Metadata richness turned an embarrassment into an actionable diagnosis; opacity leaves
products merely wrong.

The learned-fusion results sharpen both messages. For responders: the practical fusion
recipe is a *weighted* vote (the logistic weights are publishable as a lookup), worth ~40%
over flat voting. For providers: the geography baseline is the bar to clear and report —
a product whose building-level skill matches a coastline map adds value only in
combination, and provider-side validation against such a baseline would surface this before
release, not after. Spatial error statistics offer a complementary per-zone diagnostic:
local indicators of spatial association (LISA) applied to the damage-adjusted residuals
turn each product's region into a reliability *surface* — 78–86% of every product's
territory shows locally random error (the benign regime), with failures concentrated in
identifiable pockets: Microsoft's western false-positive cluster, one product's
agricultural-zone hallucinations, and a radar product's blind-spot clump that no
precision-recall table could reveal. Such surfaces are directly publishable as a
"which products to trust here" layer, and suggest *reliability-aware* fusion — weighting
votes by local error structure — as the natural next step beyond this paper.

One tempting shortcut does not work, and we log it so others need not retry it: spatial
signatures of the flags *themselves* — their rate, their clustering, even their
cross-product agreement — do not predict measured reliability across areas (all
correlations non-significant over fifteen product-area pairs). Two structural reasons:
pathological flags cluster exactly as real damage does, so clustering statistics cannot
separate a severity gradient from a land-cover artifact without reference data; and
cross-product agreement, the decisive signal at *building* level, fails at *area* level
because products' failure zones overlap. Error decorrelation is a per-building property,
not a per-region one — reliability assessment beyond a reference's coverage therefore
requires either field/crowd data (as used here) or reliability models trained across
multiple events.

**For evaluators**, the multi-reference design carried more weight than any single number:
the crowd data adjudicated a product-vs-reference dispute (the Microsoft west cluster), the
field data quantified the expert reference's own grade-dependent gaps, and their
combination converted "precision" from a fixed number into a bounded interval
(floor-to-adjusted). Consensus doubles as a reference-gap detector: the set of unanimous
flags without expert corroboration is, empirically, mostly real damage — a candidate
field-validation queue for the reference provider itself.

## Limitations

Single event, single (coastal, dense-urban) geography: the specific rule orderings and
magnitudes should not be assumed to transfer, and the cross-vs-same-sensor contrast rests
on one same-sensor pair; replication (e.g., the 2025 Myanmar earthquake, which has a
comparable product and crowd-validation landscape) is the natural next test. The consensus
analysis inherits the shared footprint base: co-flagging fails for alignment reasons as
well as disagreement, so unanimous-rule recall is understated. Crowd volunteers are not
damage-assessment experts, and their imagery vintage was not fully documented; field
reports are undated, positives-only, and skewed toward destruction (79% "complete").
The learned-fusion weights are an in-event calibration, not a transferable model — trained
and validated within one earthquake's product mix and imagery vintages. Confidence
intervals on headline numbers, population-weighted (rather than building-count)
prioritisation, and the timeliness axis — how each product's availability date interacts
with its accuracy — are in progress and absent from this draft. Two members' input imagery
details (UH, LIST) await provider confirmation.

## Conclusion

Six damage products that disagree building-by-building agree — usefully, measurably —
about where an earthquake did its worst, and their disagreement itself, structured by
sensing modality, is an exploitable signal: agreement count is a confidence dial that a
responder can set. The instruments that made this legible were not better single products
but better *references* — three imperfect datasets whose failure modes cancel. The
practical asks that follow are modest: publish analysed extents, publish confidence and
corroboration metadata, and treat crowd and field validation as first-class parts of the
product ecosystem rather than afterthoughts. The harder finding stands regardless: as of
this event, everything — products and references alike — sees destruction, not damage.

## Reproducibility note {.unnumbered}

All analyses run from immutable data snapshots (frozen 2026-07-15) in the project's
open-format data lake; per-question scripts, running notes, and the full findings register
(including every negative and superseded result) accompany this draft in the project
repository. Matching, voting, and adjudication code totals ~1,500 lines of Python against
DuckDB/GeoPandas; no analysis requires proprietary software.
